t: Introduction: capabilities of the histological method
n: In this lecture we will consider the capabilities of the histological method. Autopsy and histology remain the mainstay of examination. Nevertheless, in 10–15% of cases the cause of death is not established even after full examination. Immunohistochemistry, that is IHC, finds change not visible with ordinary staining. Fibronectin shows ischaemia within 1 hour, whereas haematoxylin–eosin, that is H&E, is still negative at that time. The accuracy of ordinary histology in determining the vitality of an injury is only 66%. Staining with glycophorin A finds extravasation of blood considerably more reliably. IHC requires the experience of a specialist and a longer processing time, but shows the vital reaction and the time of injury more precisely.

t: Two sources and the lecture plan
n: The lecture relies on two sources. The first considers biomarkers in cardiac death: protein, peptide, inflammatory and molecular signs. The second is devoted to determining the vitality of an injury in a putrefied body using glycophorin A, that is GPA; in it 16 studies were analysed. The idea linking them is that the diagnostic value is highest when immunohistochemistry is added to histology. The chain of the plan: first, sudden cardiac death, definition and causes; second, autopsy and histology; third, signs of immunohistochemistry; fourth, GPA and the vitality of injury; fifth, limitations and conclusion.

t: Sudden cardiac death: definition and causes
n: Sudden cardiac death, SCD for short, is unexpected death occurring within 1 hour of the onset of a symptom, or, if unwitnessed, within 24 hours. It makes up about 15–20% of natural deaths, 4–5 million deaths a year. Attention: after full examination 10–15% of cases remain without a cause, that is autopsy-negative. The main causes differ by age. In persons over 35, coronary artery disease is commoner, whereas in young patients cardiomyopathy, myocarditis and inherited arrhythmia are commoner.

t: The problem of autopsy-negative death
n: Pay attention to the problem of autopsy-negative death. Sudden cardiac death accounts for about 15–20 per cent of natural deaths, and worldwide is associated with about 4–5 million deaths a year. Even after full autopsy and histology, 10–15% of cases remain unexplained; they are called "autopsy-negative sudden unexplained death". In such a case the family is left without a precise explanation, the court without sufficient proof, and the doctor without the information needed for prevention. Autopsy and histology remain the main method. To fill the gap, post-mortem biochemistry and molecular methods are added.

t: Case analysis: histology did not show the cause
n: Case analysis. As a teaching example, a young person died suddenly. At autopsy and on ordinary histology no clear cause of death was found. In the young, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis or inherited arrhythmic syndromes are often met, and some of their bases are not visible on ordinary histology. Next steps: immunohistochemistry, that is fibronectin, C5b-9, desmin and S100A1, then biochemistry, then gene analysis, that is molecular autopsy. Question: what can be done for family members? If a gene variant is found, cascade screening identifies relatives at risk.

t: Quick question: definition of SCD
n: Quick question. First question: within what time of onset of symptoms does death occur in the definition of SCD? Correct answer: within 1 hour in a witnessed case. In an unwitnessed case, death must occur within 24 hours of the person last being seen alive and well. Attention: there is a risk of error, 1 hour and 24 hours are not the same. The first relates to the witnessed case, the second to the unwitnessed one. The definition implies unexpected natural death, presumably of cardiac origin. In those over 35, coronary artery disease is commoner.

t: Protein markers of myocardial necrosis
n: Protein markers of myocardial necrosis. Cardiac troponins, that is cTnI and cTnT, are regarded as the most specific and sensitive marker of cardiomyocyte necrosis. Haemolysis and PMI affect them, and high-sensitivity hs-tests have widened the window; as samples, pericardial fluid and femoral vein blood are taken. Attention: CK-MB is not troponin. CK-MB, that is creatine kinase-MB, rises also in trauma, epilepsy and muscle injury, and its specificity is low. It is cheap and widely available, and is assessed together with troponin. A concordant rise in both at a short PMI, that is post-mortem time, confirms acute ischaemic death.

t: H-FABP, GPBB and the multi-marker approach
n: H-FABP, that is heart fatty acid-binding protein, is released quickly, but breaks down quickly when PMI lengthens. GPBB, that is glycogen phosphorylase BB, indicates early ischaemia; in a panel together with troponin it raises sensitivity. Therefore one moves from a single marker to a panel: for early ischaemia H-FABP and GPBB, rapid breakdown is related to lengthening PMI, a multi-marker panel is put together, it is adapted to PMI and sampling site, and as a result a probabilistic, that is relative, conclusion is obtained. Instead of an absolute value, a ratio, the ratio between pericardium and blood, as well as a panel, is more reliable; the threshold is not rigid.

t: Case analysis: pericardial fluid and blood
n: Case analysis. Unexpected death, PMI exceeds 24–48 hours, and in histology signs of ischaemia are not clear. Troponin in pericardial fluid is stable longer than in blood, so compare it with femoral vein blood. The ratio of troponin in pericardial fluid to that in femoral vein blood reduces the effect of PMI and haemolysis; it is preferable to an absolute threshold. Question: which medium and which ratio are chosen? Why may central heart blood give an artificially high value? Try to answer this question yourself.

t: Peptide markers: haemodynamic stress
n: Peptide markers reflect not necrosis but haemodynamic stress. They include B-type natriuretic peptide, that is BNP, NT-proBNP, copeptin and sST2. NT-proBNP shows ventricular stretch and remodelling, but also rises in kidney and lung disease. Copeptin indicates acute stress and haemodynamic collapse, but also rises in sepsis, trauma and stroke. sST2 reflects myocardial strain and fibrosis, but a special method is needed and it is little validated. NT-proBNP in pericardial fluid is protected from blood redistribution and is relatively stable for 24–48 hours. The strongest result is given not by a single peptide but by a multi-marker panel.

t: Case analysis: copeptin and troponin together
n: Case analysis. A patient collapsed and died soon after arrival at hospital. At autopsy no clear lesion was found, and the possibility of a missed infarction was raised. In post-mortem blood, copeptin was raised together with troponins; this showed that acute ischaemia was present at the time of the fall, as Kutlu and co-authors wrote. In this way a missed clinical diagnosis can be reconstructed later. Normal levels, however, may protect the doctor from an unfounded accusation. Question: why should copeptin be interpreted not alone but precisely together with troponin?

t: Quick question: peptides and markers of necrosis
n: Quick questions. First question: which marker shows myocardial necrosis? Answer: cardiac troponins; they are regarded as the most specific and sensitive marker. Second question: which markers show haemodynamic stress? Answer: BNP and NT-proBNP, copeptin and sST2. Attention: there is a risk of error, copeptin is not a heart-specific marker. It may rise also in sepsis, trauma and stroke, so context is needed. Copeptin does not replace troponin but supplements it. Troponin, H-FABP and copeptin together gave an accuracy above 90% for ischaemic SCD.

t: Inflammation and immunohistochemistry (IHC)
n: Inflammation and immunohistochemistry. CRP, that is C-reactive protein, and IL-6, that is interleukin-6, are soluble mediators. They may support the supposition of inflammation. Attention: CRP and IL-6 rise also in hypoxia, prolonged agony and terminal stress, that is the rise does not prove inflammation. IHC markers, however, show the vital reaction in tissue and help to stage an injury more precisely in time. Soluble cytokines are cheap, but break down and are distorted by bacterial overgrowth. IHC requires skill and time, but together with histology gives the strongest result.

t: IHC signs of early ischaemia
n: IHC signs of early ischaemia. These markers help to identify early ischaemia not visible with H&E staining, that is haematoxylin and eosin. Fibronectin accumulates at the sarcolemma and is regarded as an early sign. C5b-9 is detected in acute ischaemic death; in non-ischaemic or chronic conditions it is absent, and it shows that the cell was alive during ischaemia. Disruption of desmin fibres is seen. In S100A1, immunoreactivity disappears. Attention: C5b-9 is a sign of accumulation, S100A1 a sign of disappearance; both indicate ischaemia.

t: Time axis: H&E negative, IHC positive
n: We consider the time axis. Coronary occlusion begins, and in the first hour no change is visible on H&E staining, but on IHC fibronectin is detected. Fibronectin staining shows damage within 1 hour of occlusion, while H&E is still negative. S100A1 reactivity too may disappear in about an hour. So negative H&E does not exclude ischaemia; IHC gives additional evidence.

t: Myocarditis and systemic diseases
n: Myocarditis and systemic diseases. Systemic sclerosis causes diffuse fibrosis and microvascular disturbance in the myocardium; this may end in fatal arrhythmia. Cardiac sarcoidosis is an important cause of unexplained sudden death: in cases initially "autopsy-negative", granulomatous infiltration was found in the conduction system. In patients who died in the COVID-19 period, it is documented that SARS-CoV-2 damaged the endothelium of coronary microvessels; death occurred even without clear myocarditis. In children, Kawasaki disease and MIS-C, that is multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, are associated with fatal arrhythmias and coronary vasculitis.

t: Comparing soluble markers and IHC
n: We compare soluble markers and IHC. CRP and IL-6 are easily found and cheap, but specificity is low; they rise in myocarditis and sepsis, and also in hypoxia and prolonged agony, and are prone to breakdown. IHC markers: fibronectin, C5b-9, desmin and S100A1. Their processing lasts longer and requires special technical skill, but specificity is high and they show the vital reaction. They show ischaemia early. The strongest result: IHC together with histology; soluble markers are supplementary evidence.

t: Case analysis: ordinary stain negative, IHC positive
n: Case analysis. A person died suddenly, and at autopsy there is no clear cause. On H&E staining, signs of myocarditis or ischaemia are not clear. Fibronectin may show ischaemia within 1 hour of coronary occlusion, when H&E is still negative. Loss of S100A1 is also an early sign. Deposition of C5b-9 was found in acute ischaemic death, and is absent in a non-ischaemic or chronic state; it shows cardiomyocyte viability. Question: which markers will you choose in the IHC panel, and why are CRP or IL-6 alone insufficient?

t: MicroRNA and molecular traces
n: Molecular traces. MicroRNA, miRNA for short, is a short RNA regulating gene expression. It is tissue-specific and gives a stable profile up to 72 hours after death. The heart-specific miR-1, miR-133, miR-208 and miR-499 are raised in ischaemic sudden death and agree with troponin and necrosis. Exosomal miRNA is protected inside vesicles; it distinguishes ischaemic death from non-cardiac death better, and a stored sample can be re-analysed. Proteomics and metabolomics show mitochondrial disturbance, but depend on PMI. Multicentre verification and standardisation are needed.

t: Molecular autopsy: NGS and genes
n: In molecular autopsy, NGS, that is next-generation sequencing, has expanded from a gene panel to examination of the whole exome, WES, and the whole genome, WGS. Channelopathy genes: SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNH2, RYR2. Cardiomyopathy genes: PKP2, DSP, MYH7, LMNA, DES. Pathogenic variants were found in 20–30% of autopsy-negative cases. Variants of uncertain significance, that is VUS, may account for up to half. The chain: autopsy and histology negative, NGS, variant pathogenic or VUS, cascade screening of relatives, then genetic counselling and prevention.

t: Case analysis: a structurally normal heart
n: Case analysis. A young person died suddenly. The heart appears normal to the eye, and in histology too no clear change was found. Such a case is called "autopsy-negative sudden unexplained death". In the source it makes up 10–15% of cases. Genetic predisposition may appear before structural change and trigger a fatal arrhythmia; the genes of channelopathies and cardiomyopathies are examined. Question: if a pathogenic variant is found, what benefit does it give relatives, and what problems arise over consent and confidentiality?

t: Quick question: histology and molecular methods
n: Quick questions. First question: if no change is seen on haematoxylin and eosin staining, what shows early ischaemia? Answer: immunohistochemistry, that is fibronectin, C5b-9, desmin, S100A1. Second question: was the injury inflicted during life? Answer: anti-glycophorin A immunohistochemistry; the accuracy of ordinary histology was only 66%. Third question: and if autopsy and histology do not show the cause? Answer: molecular autopsy with NGS, that is analysis of channelopathy and cardiomyopathy genes. Attention: a biomarker is dynamic, a cellular response before death; a genetic variant, however, is a stable change in DNA. Do not confuse these two levels.

t: Pre-analytical factors: sample and PMI
n: Pre-analytical factors. Femoral vein blood is preferred; central heart blood, because of seepage from the myocardium, may show artificially raised values. Attention: haemolysis falsely raises CK-MB and LDH, and bacteria IL-6 and CRP, mimicking inflammation. According to the table, pericardial fluid is isolated and stable, but early aspiration is needed. Vitreous humour is resistant to haemolysis and putrefaction and is useful for copeptin. By PMI, troponin is measurable for more than 48 hours, while H-FABP breaks down faster. Storage: aseptic sample, centrifuge, −80 °C for molecular analysis; exclude a spoiled sample.

t: Pre-analytical and post-analytical interpretation: sample, storage, ratio
n: Interpretation of post-mortem biomarkers, Sacco and co-authors 2026, section 7. Femoral vein blood is preferred; central heart blood, because of leakage from the myocardium, may give an artificially high value. Pericardial fluid is a reliable alternative for NT-proBNP and troponin, and vitreous humour is useful for peptides such as copeptin. Storage: aseptic femoral vein sample, fluoride tube, centrifuge, −80 °C for molecular analysis; dried blood spot cards for DNA and RNA. Clinical cut-off values are not applied after death: the pericardium-to-blood ratio and Bayesian models give a probabilistic conclusion. Troponin is measurable for more than 48 hours, and H-FABP breaks down faster.

t: Forensic and legal aspects
n: Forensic and legal aspects. In insurance disputes, biomarker data have reduced the share of unexplained deaths. On the question of a cut-off after death there is no general threshold; the solution is a probabilistic model adjusted for PMI. The Daubert criteria require reproducibility, peer review and a known error rate; the solution is standardisation and validation. In malpractice claims there is the question of delayed diagnosis of infarction, and the biomarker serves both prosecution and defence. In genetic data the problem is consent, confidentiality and informing relatives, and a consent model is needed for governance. In Italy, a case closed more than 20 years earlier was reopened because of an anti-GPA result.

t: Case analysis: sudden death in hospital
n: Case analysis. A patient collapses and dies soon after arriving at hospital, and at autopsy no clear change is found. An accusation of late detection of infarction arises. As Kutlu and co-authors showed, in post-mortem blood copeptin rose together with troponin; this showed acute ischaemia at the collapse and restored the missed diagnosis. Conversely, normal levels protect the doctor: death may have occurred suddenly from arrhythmia. Biomarkers are a double-edged weapon for prosecution and defence. Question: can a rise in copeptin be the sole evidence? No: it is not heart-specific, it rises also in sepsis, trauma and stroke; and there is no universal post-mortem threshold either.

t: Practical sequence: from circumstances to molecular analysis
n: The practical sequence goes from circumstances to molecular analysis. The first step is the circumstances data and autopsy: the circumstances data replace the history, and autopsy is a stage like first-line imaging. The second step is histology and IHC: fibronectin, C5b-9, desmin and S100A1 show early ischaemia. The third step is biochemistry: troponin and NT-proBNP. If no explanation is found, the fourth step is molecular analysis: miRNA and NGS, that is next-generation sequencing. At the end, the final conclusion combines all the information.

t: The future: multi-omics and artificial intelligence
n: About the future. A single marker does not give final proof; signs of necrosis, stress, inflammation and molecular signs are combined. At present single markers are mainly used, and in the future multi-marker panels are expected. Laboratory protocols currently differ, and in the future internationally harmonised guidelines are needed. Diagnosis is at present divided into separate histology, biochemistry and imaging, and in the future a digital-molecular autopsy combining imaging, histology, biochemistry, genomics and modelling is expected. Artificial intelligence has shown more than 90% in experiment, but transparency is lacking. It must be transparent and explainable; "black box" models may not pass in court.

t: Glycophorin A (GPA): what it is and why it is needed
n: What glycophorin A is and why it is needed. Glycophorins are a family of glycoproteins of the erythrocyte, that is red blood cell, membrane. They include GPA, GPB, GPC and GPD. GPA is the commonest glycophorin; it maintains the shape and flexibility of the erythrocyte and is also called CD235a. The anti-GPA antibody in IHC shows the erythrocyte in tissue and is resistant to putrefaction; for this reason it helps to distinguish a vital injury from a post-mortem one. Attention: there is a risk of error, glycophorin is also found in bone marrow and in foci of extramedullary haematopoiesis. This may give a false positive result.

t: The logic of GPA: vitality of injury
n: The logic of GPA is based on determining the vitality of an injury. Staining with anti-GPA is performed. If the erythrocyte lies outside a vessel, GPA is positive; this means that circulation was active, that is the injury was inflicted while circulation was still active, an ante-mortem injury. Negative GPA shows the absence of erythrocytes in the tissue; this supports a post-mortem origin of the injury. Attention: hypostasis gives a false bruise; in cadaveric lividity the GPA reaction was not positive.

t: Methodology of the systematic review
n: Methodology of the systematic review. The search was carried out in the PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases. The review was performed on the basis of the international guideline PRISMA, that is reporting of systematic reviews. Stages of selection: 799 findings, 459 without duplicates, 50 by abstract, then full text was assessed and 16 works were included. Of these 16 works, 10 were case, series and control studies, 2 experimental and 4 narrative reviews.

t: Results: GPA and the accuracy of ordinary histology
n: We turn to the results. In the review 50 samples were analysed: 42 cases and 8 control samples. Forty-eight samples were stained with anti-GPA and 2 with anti-GPC. The GPA result agreed fully with the presence of blood, and in one case could not be assessed. The accuracy of ordinary histology, however, was 66%. According to the table, cases in which blood was present but not found made up 18%, and indeterminate results 16%.

t: GPA review: demography of the samples and degree of putrefaction
n: GPA review: demography of the samples, Donato and co-authors 2025. In all, 50 samples: 42 cases and 8 controls; 48 stained with anti-GPA and 2 with anti-GPC. By sex, 11 men, 12 women, and in 26 not clear. Age was known in only 31 cases, from 2 weeks to 88 years, median 57. PMI is known in 42 cases; in 64 per cent of cases putrefaction was severe. PMI and degree of putrefaction do not always agree. The risk of bias was assessed by JBI critical appraisal checklists: the methodological quality of the included studies was "fair".

t: Putrefied tissue, bone and other samples
n: In putrefied tissue, bone and other samples, GPA may remain positive. In Bertozzi's study, all injury samples of putrefied bodies were GPA-positive. In exhumation of 8 bodies, PMI 621–878 days, GPA was positive in 11 samples. In fracture of macerated bone, that is bone softened in water, all three were positive in 3 cases. In a partly skeletonised body, only 1 injury was GPA-positive. The sample of Amussat's sign was taken from a non-putrefied, hanged body, in the carotid artery: not found on H&E, present on GPA. It is not an example of a putrefied state.

t: Case analysis: a case reopened in Italy
n: Case analysis. In Italy, after more than 20 years, an old case was reopened. The body was examined twice separately, the first diagnosis being suicide. At the second examination GPA was applied: injuries linked to death were negative, and the soft tissues of the neck, that is the laryngotracheal region, were positive. The result in the neck was consistent with violent mechanical asphyxia, and the first diagnosis lost its force. The court passed a guilty verdict, not yet final. Question: what changed at the second autopsy, and how did GPA affect this change?

t: Quick question: interpreting GPA
n: Quick questions. First question: what does a negative reaction for GPA mean? It shows the absence of erythrocytes and supports that the injury arose after death. Positive GPA shows erythrocytes outside the vessel: the injury was formed while circulation was active, that is vital, ante-mortem. In healthy skin GPA is positive only inside vessels. In a bruise and injured muscle, erythrocytes are seen to have left the vessel, that is extravasation. Attention: risk of error. Hypostasis or pseudo-bruising is not a vital injury. Pooling of blood under gravity may look like an injury.

t: GPA IHC protocol
n: The GPA IHC protocol is performed in the following sequence. A section 4 μm thick is cut from a paraffin block and H&E is also done; the slide is coated with 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane. For pretreatment, for antigen retrieval, it is boiled in EDTA buffer. The primary antibody, that is anti-GPA, is used at a dilution of 1:500 for 120 minutes. For detection the LSAB+ kit is used: the biotinylated secondary antibody binds to streptavidin with peroxidase. Finally it is stained with Mayer's haematoxylin and viewed under the microscope.

t: Limitations and forensic criteria
n: Limitations and forensic criteria. A false negative result arises from incorrect sampling, and a false positive from tissues with erythroid cells, such as bone marrow. Studies are few, 16 included; there is no recent double-blind study; for GPC there are only 2 works. Reliability depends on correct methodology and a qualified laboratory. The Daubert criteria are applied in the USA and are four: foundation, that is the scientific principle or validity of the method; application, that is correct use of the method; fit, that is information useful for reconstructing the event; and acceptance, that is recognition of the information by specialists.

t: Conclusion: potential of the histological method
n: We summarise. Immunohistochemistry, through fibronectin, C5b-9, desmin and S100A1, helps to identify early ischaemia and myocarditis not visible with ordinary staining. Glycophorin A, by the IHC method, finds haemorrhage even in a putrefied body. The accuracy of ordinary histology was 66%, and agreement with GPA was complete. If histology is insufficient, microRNA and next-generation sequencing, that is NGS, are added. However, standard threshold values and multicentre confirmation are still lacking. The reliability of the GPA result depends on correct methodology and a qualified laboratory. Studies are few, so a single protocol is needed.
